title: Editor’s Pick: New Children’s Picture Books
summary: Let these stories remind you to enjoy the goodness of the moment and, even as it changes to something new, that God’s goodness is everlasting.
summary_zh: 让这些故事提醒你享受当下的美好，即使它变成了新的东西，神的美好是永恒的。
title_zh: 编辑精选：全新儿童图画书
content: Autumn is a season of changes. At our home, as the leaves yellowed and the days shortened, my youngest child started middle school. That means picture books have me feeling a little nostalgia for the past these days, right alongside a lot of excitement for new things to come. Many of these books are about big changes and adjusting to them, like living with a new baby, moving to a new place, or finding a new heart in Christ’s kingdom. But some are also about the little changes happening around us every day, like laughter over a fleeting moment of childhood imagination or settling down to sleep to prepare for a new day. With all these experiences arriving on the horizon and then flying past like interstate billboards, it’s sweet to remember that “every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow due to change” (James 1:17). As you hand one of these brand-new books to a young reader or curl up to enjoy it together, let these stories remind you to enjoy the goodness of the moment, even as it is changing to something new, and that God’s goodness is everlasting. 1. God Gives Sleep by Betsy Childs Howard, illustrated by Bethan Welby ( TGC Store | Amazon) When our family was exhausted and planning a big move with four children ages 6 and under, I really could have used this little book from Betsy Childs Howard. God Gives Sleep is a rhyming board book with illustrations of adorable animals (sleeping ladybugs!) and two simple refrains that even very young listeners can repeat or “read” for themselves: “God gives sleep” and “God will keep.” Both reflect promises from God that feel vital to the early days of parenting filled with sweet, sleepy snuggles and long, sleepless nights. The last picture shows the entire family asleep and includes Isaiah 40:31 (“Those who hope in the LORD will renew their strength,” NIV). God Gives Sleep is engaging, gentle, funny, and wise, and I’ve already given it to parents of new babies. 2. Winnie-the-Pooh: The Graphic Novel by A. A. Milne, adapted by Kevan Chandler and Joe Sutphin ( Amazon ) Full disclosure: I’m a huge Pooh fan. I’ve probably read the original Milne book dozens of times, and I can be a little sniffy about adaptations. But I loved this one. While I missed Milne’s distinctive narration in parts of the storytelling, this graphic novel retains enough of the original language and has such beautiful artwork that it easily justifies its existence. Parents of young independent readers often ask me for recommendations for books complex enough to be engaging but with content and formatting suitable for early elementary school. This version perfectly fits that space where 6-to-9-year-olds can track the story through the pictures but also enjoy the challenge of some complex vocabulary (“Sudden and Temporary Immersion”) and jokes that reward context research (“An ambush is a sort of Surprise.” “So is a gorse-bush sometimes.”). Winnie-the-Pooh: The Graphic Novel is a sweet and worthy tribute to this classic celebration of early childhood in all its imaginative wonder. 3. The Upside-Down, Inside-Out, Can’t-Believe-It Kingdom by Jonathan Landry Cruse, illustrated by Joe Hox ( Amazon ) The adventure begins with a son begging his father to tell him an exciting bedtime story with dragons and knights. The result is this retelling of the gospel as a quest with a king and a prince and a reminder of our humble place in the kingdom. Joe Hox’s illustrations stand out for being traditional and bright, with a dragon that isn’t too fierce for younger readers but also enough detail within the pictures to engage older readers. The story tells us that the good King will “make us be strong with the strength of His might,” a powerful message for young knights who want to do great things for the kingdom. 4. Doing Something New: A Prayer for Beginnings by Mitali Perkins, illustrated by Andrés Landazábal ( Amazon ) Mitali Perkins includes a n
content_zh:
秋为一季之变. 在家中,随着叶子被黄了,日子被缩短,我最小的孩子开始上中学. 这意味着图书让我觉得过去有些怀旧, 与很多刺激 来的新事物。

这些书中很多是关于大变化并适应它们,比如与新婴儿一起生活,搬到新地方,或者在基督的王国中找到新的心. 但有些人也谈到我们周围每天发生的小变化,比如在童年短暂的想象中欢笑,或者沉睡以准备新的一天。

随着所有这些经历的到来,然后像州际告示牌一样飞过,令人欣慰的是,“每一个好的礼物和完美的礼物都是来自上面,来自灯之父,与他一起没有变化或阴影。” (詹姆斯1:17)。

当你把这些全新的书交给一个年轻的读者 或整理起来一起欣赏的时候, 让这些故事提醒你享受这一刻的美好, 即使它正在变成新的事物, 上帝的善良是永恒的。 1. 联合国

由Bethan Welby(TGC Store QQ Amazon)所展示, 当家庭精疲力竭,计划一个大动作 四个孩子6岁和6岁以下, 我真的可以用这本小书 从贝茜 Childs Howard。

上帝赐予睡眠(God Gives Sleep)是一本配有可爱动物(sleeping ladybugs!)插图的韵律板书,还有两个简单的节奏,即使非常年轻的听众也能为自己重复或“阅读 ” : “ 上帝赐予睡眠 ” 和“上帝会保留 ” 。 两者都反映了上帝的诺言,这些诺言对养育孩子的早期至关重要,充满了甜蜜的,沉睡的和漫长的,无眠的夜晚.

最后一张图片显示整个家庭都睡了,包括以赛亚40:31(“那些希望被耶和华唤起力量的人”,NIV)。 上帝赐予睡眠的热情、温和、幽默和智慧, 由Kevan Chandler和Joe Sutphin(亚马逊)改编 全面披露:我是一个巨大的维尼粉丝。

我可能读过Milne的原作数十次, 但我爱这个 虽然我错过了Milne在故事部分的突出叙事,

年轻独立读者的家长经常向我征求关于书本复杂到足以参与,但内容和格式适合初等学校的建议。

这一版本完全适合6至9岁的人通过图片追踪故事的空间,但也享受一些复杂词汇的挑战(“突然和暂时的印象”)和奖励上下文研究的笑话(“埋伏是一种惊喜”)。 “有时粗鲁也是。 ”

title: How Memorizing the Sermon on the Mount Reorders My Heart
summary: In a world where algorithms capture our affections and lure us online via our cravings, one of the most effective resistance strategies we can employ is to study and memorize Scripture—especially the Sermon on the Mount.
summary_zh: 在一个算法捕捉我们的感情并通过我们的渴望在网上引诱我们的世界里，我们可以使用的最有效的抵抗策略之一是学习和背诵圣经，尤其是登山宝训。
title_zh: 背诵登山宝训如何重塑我的心
content: A couple of years ago, two college students challenged me—a woman in her 50s—to memorize the Sermon on the Mount (Matt. 5–7). Inwardly, I balked, but now I know that few things in my 35 years of following Jesus have been more transformative than committing Jesus’s most famous sermon to memory. John Stott wrote that the Sermon on the Mount is “the nearest thing to a manifesto that [Jesus] ever uttered, for it is his own description of what he wanted his followers to be and to do.” After spending the last few years memorizing it, I see with increasing clarity that I need Jesus’s help to live out what he taught. In a world where algorithms capture our affections and lure us online via our cravings, one of the most effective resistance strategies we can employ is to study and memorize Scripture—especially the Sermon on the Mount. Create a New Algorithm The algorithm often knows us better than we know ourselves. Every time we buy something on Amazon or pause to watch a reel on social media, the algorithm chronicles our activities and builds a profile of us. This profile shows our real interests (not just the ones we list in our social media bios) and some of our most private behaviors (the ones we thank God aren’t live streamed). In milliseconds, companies use what the algorithm knows about us to discover the most effective way to get us to buy their products. In the same way that the algorithm learns about us with each post we like and each reel we watch, God’s Word comes alive in us with every command we learn and put into practice, with every verse we ponder, and with every teaching we adopt as a way of life. By absorbing and obeying Jesus’s Sermon on the Mount, we can create a feedback loop that enlarges his kingdom rule over our lives. Let Scripture Reorder Your Heart Before I started my memorization project, I’d heard many Christians tout Scripture memory as one of the most potent tools for conforming to Jesus, but I didn’t take it seriously. All that changed when I realized algorithms had more access to my life than God’s Word did. By absorbing and obeying Jesus’s Sermon on the Mount, we can create a feedback loop that enlarges his kingdom rule over our lives. Like many Americans, I was averaging more than two hours daily scrolling social media and shopping online, and much less time reading the Bible. I’d thought lack of time was my biggest obstacle to memorizing Scripture. But in reality, my affections and priorities were the obstacle. Memorizing and studying the Sermon on the Mount has provided a powerful reset. I’ve noticed two significant changes in my life. 1. My thoughts are increasingly populated by Jesus’s desires for me. Previously, I was easily shaped by what internet influencers said I should be doing and what my heart really wanted to do. Now, Scripture tenderly draws me to Christ’s transforming grace. For example, a few months ago, someone wrote harsh words to me. I couldn’t sidestep what I’d memorized: Pray for those who hurt you (Mt. 5:44) In those difficult interactions, Jesus’s teaching gave me wisdom to stop reacting and start praying for the one lashing out. Pausing to pray breaks down my self-protective stance so I can consider what the log in my eye might be (Mt. 7:5). 2. I see how vastly different God’s kingdom is from the world we live in. I no longer feel as drawn to the shallow version of perfection the algorithm offers me—the beautiful home, the perfectly fit woman charmingly dressed, or the promise of perpetual travel. When I stop to linger over another picture-perfect kitchen, the Sermon on the Mount prompts me to consider where my treasure really is. These chapters have given me a robust lens through which I can view all of God’s Word. After drinking so deeply of Jesus’s sermon , I see it as the hinge on which both the Old Testament and the New Testament hang. 几年前,两个大学生挑战我——一个50多岁的女性——要记住山上赛门(Matt. 5-7). 但现在我知道,在我追随耶稣的35年里, 没有什么事情比把耶稣最出名的布道当作记忆更具有变革性。

约翰·斯托特(John Stott)写道:"山上赛蒙是[耶稣]曾经发表的宣言中最接近的东西,因为这是他自己对追随者所希望的和所要做的事的描述". 我越来越清楚地看到,我需要耶稣的帮助来维持他所教的。

每次我们购买亚马逊或暂停观看社交媒体的片段, 算法记录我们的活动, 以及一些最私人的行为(我们感谢上帝的人不是活生生的)。

之前,我很容易被网络影响者 说我应该做什么 和我的心真正想要做什么。 现在,《圣经》轻而易举地吸引我走向基督的恩典。 例如,几个月前,有人给我写了严厉的话. 我无法回避我所记住的:为伤害你的人祈祷(Mt.

5:44 在困难的交往中,耶稣的教导给了我智慧,让我停止反应,开始为那一次狂欢祈祷. 暂停祈祷 打破自我保护的姿势 这样我就可以考虑我的眼中可能是什么(7:5山) 2. 我看到上帝的王国与我们生活的世界大相径庭。

我不再觉得算法能吸引到我的 浅薄的完美版本, 当我停止停留 停留在另一个图片完美的厨房, 山上赛门 促使我考虑 我的宝藏到底在哪里。

title: Who Is the God of the Bible?
summary: Contemplating God’s names provides a deeper understanding of his being and attributes and a firmer foundation for our faith and hope.
summary_zh: 沉思神的名字可以更深入地了解祂的存在和属性，并为我们的信心和希望奠定更坚实的基础。
title_zh: 谁是圣经中的神？
content: According to the Belgic Confession , God reveals himself to us in two “books”: the book of nature (God’s world) and the book of Scripture (God’s written Word). The primary way God reveals himself in the book of Scripture is by proclaiming his name. In this first of two paired lectures from TGC25, Scott Swain considers several of the names whereby God reveals himself in the Bible. Contemplating God’s names provides a deeper understanding of his being and attributes and a firmer foundation for our faith and hope. It also helps us better appreciate the ways God reveals himself to us in Jesus Christ. 根据贝尔吉克的忏悔书,上帝在两个"书"中向我们揭示了自己:自然之书(真主的世界)和天经之书(真主所写的文字). 神在"通典"中主要揭示自己的方式是宣布自己的名字. 在TGC25的两次对口讲座中,斯科特·斯温(Scott Swain)首先考虑了上帝在"圣经"中揭示自己的几个名字.

质疑上帝的名声为人们更深入地了解他的存在和属性,并为我们的信仰和希望打下更坚实的基础。 这也帮助我们更好地理解上帝在耶稣基督中向我们揭示自己的方式.

title: ‘I Play Rocky’ Finds New Inspiration in an Old Story
summary: ‘I Play Rocky’ is the latest pop-culture celebration of storytelling as agency: telling your story in just the way you want it to be told.
summary_zh: “I Play Rocky”是将讲故事作为代理的最新流行文化庆祝活动：以您希望的方式讲述您的故事。
title_zh: 《我扮演洛基》在古老的故事中寻找新的灵感
content: Rocky debuted in theaters 50 years ago, in 1976—a bicentennial-year release that underscored the movie’s profound American spirit. Immediately a blockbuster and critical darling (the highest-grossing movie of 1976 and winner of the Best Picture Oscar), it has since become a pantheon film in American cinema. Rocky ’s Philadelphia setting and underdog, rags-to-riches story captured a hardscrabble American optimism, something that gave needed inspiration in the mid-1970s and resonates still today. Now in 2026—America’s semiquincentennial— Rocky is getting a theatrical rerelease. And a new movie, I Play Rocky (out today in select theaters) is telling the story of the iconic movie’s development, which is an underdog epic of its own. The movie, directed by Peter Farrelly ( Green Book ) and starring Anthony Ippolito in a breakout turn as Sylvester Stallone, is a refreshingly feel-good crowd pleaser. It’s the sort of well-made, intelligent, but also inspiring movie for grown-ups that feels like a dying breed in Hollywood. Movies About Moviemaking I Play Rocky (rated PG-13 for language) follows a well-worn template of a movie about the making of a classic movie. Saving Mr. Banks (2013) was about Walt Disney and the making of Mary Poppins . Hitchcock (2012) was about Alfred Hitchcock and the making of Psycho . Last year’s Nouvelle Vague was about Jean-Luc Godard and the making of Breathless . I Play Rocky is about Stallone and the making of Rocky . Hollywood loves making movies about itself: stories about storytelling, movies about moviemaking, actors playing actors. Hollywood loves making movies about itself: stories about storytelling, movies about moviemaking, actors playing actors. Self-reflexive inspiration goes back more than a century in cinema, perhaps starting with Dziga Vertov’s Man with a Movie Camera (1929). The 1950s produced classics like Sunset Boulevard (1950) and Singin’ in the Rain (1952), but the trend really picked up in the postmodern era in the 1960s and beyond: 8 ½ (1963), Day for Night (1973), Mulholland Drive (2001), Adaptation (2002), The Artist (2011), and Once Upon a Time . . . in Hollywood (2019). The list is long. A hallmark of postmodernity is a metaposture of knowing awareness—storytellers who know they’re storytellers and want the audience to know that they know. As postmodernism has given way to metamodernism , the trend of “movies about moviemaking” has continued, but in a slightly different register. These sorts of films are no longer merely metaexercises in self-awareness. The cerebral, cynical detachment of “films about filmmaking” like Barton Fink (1991), Ed Wood (1994), or even Who Framed Roger Rabbit (1988) has given way to metamodern expressions that blend cynicism and sincerity, self-awareness with earnest escapism. Steven Spielberg’s The Fabelmans (2022) is a recent example of a movie in this vein, and I Play Rocky has a similar feel. Even as it lifts the veil on the Hollywood myth factory and mines many laughs out of the fundamentally profit-seeking, money-centric nature of the movie business, it’s full of heart and soul. It has a joyful, hopeful, sincere, perhaps idealistic spirit (“I’d rather be an optimist and be wrong, than a pessimist and be right,” one character says). Refreshing Celebration of Marriage I also like how I Play Rocky celebrates the empowering beauty of marriage. The film opens with Stallone as a broke actor in New York, sometimes sleeping on the streets and at one point accepting a role in an X-rated adult film just to earn some desperately needed money (a dark part of Stallone’s past that the film plays for awkward laughs). He’s a lost soul with bleak prospects. But then he meets Sasha (AnnaSophia Robb), with whom he works at a movie theater. They get married and move to Los Angeles, and things start to turn around for him. As a husband and soon a father, Stallone feels more urgency to provide. title: How the Lord’s Supper Fuels Spiritual Growth
summary: Calvin shows us that the Lord’s Supper is fuel for spiritual growth, so we should come to the table expectantly every time.
summary_zh: 加尔文向我们表明，主的晚餐是灵性成长的燃料，所以我们每次都应该期待地来到餐桌前。
title_zh: 主的晚餐如何促进灵性成长
content: Recently, I (and my peers) have experienced a number of parishioners converting to Catholicism. As I’ve talked to these converts, they’ve consistently brought up the Lord’s Table. They find encouragement in identifying the bread and wine with Jesus’s body and blood. I’ve heard statements such as this: Pastor George, I like the idea that Jesus was talking about the Lord’s supper when he said, “Whoever feeds on my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him” (John 6:56). My faith just feels more real if I’m literally bringing Jesus into my body on a daily basis. While this phenomenon seems to be happening with greater frequency, it’s not totally new. Years ago, I served alongside a man at an ordination service for another pastor in our city. I hadn’t met this man before; I only knew he had until recently been a professor at a Reformed and evangelical seminary. This man preached a solid message on Jesus’s call for ministers of the gospel, and I thanked him for it. Then, the next day, I saw him being interviewed on TV. I tuned in just as he explained, I needed more realism than my tradition provided, so during lunch I would walk down to the local Roman Catholic parish and take the Eucharist. To unite literally with Jesus’s body and blood was more deeply satisfying to me than the “mystery of union with Christ” my church taught. So, I resigned my post at the seminary and went home to Rome. I could relate other conversations with those who have left the Reformed faith and joined the Roman Catholic, Orthodox, or Anglo-Catholic traditions. A similar theme runs through them all: the desire for a more transformational, sensory reality than what the Reformed view of the Lord’s supper provides. Is this critique valid? How would John Calvin respond to the critique that if you follow the Reformed view of the supper, you’re missing out on its power? Transformed at the Table Sometimes, in an effort to have biblically faithful theology, Reformed Christians speak only of what the communion elements are not . I’m painfully aware of my of shortcomings in this regard. This can inadvertently drive some believers to seek out a more “real” experience in other traditions. We can get caught up in debating the exact nature of the bread and wine and forget to ask the more pressing question: How should this meal change me today? Let’s look back at Calvin’s teachings on communion. When we do, we’ll recover a renewed vision for the table, one that sees it as a divine encounter that motivates a transformed life of profound gratitude and obedience. In short, Calvin shows us that the Lord’s supper is fuel for spiritual growth, so we should come to the table expectantly every time. In Calvin’s “ Short Treatise on the Lord’s Supper ,” he writes that the supper fuels the believer’s spiritual growth in at least three ways. 1. The supper assures us of our inheritance in Christ. Calvin teaches that Jesus uses his table to assure us of our inheritance. He doesn’t merely mean that the supper gives us a psychological boost. He means that assurance comes by means of a real union between Christ and the believer, and he means that our experience of this union is expedited by faithfully partaking in the covenant meal. Calvin shows us that the Lord’s supper is fuel for spiritual growth, so we should come to the table expectantly every time. In his commentary on Ephesians, Calvin writes , “Paul says that we are members of his [Christ’s] flesh and of his bones. Do we wonder then, that in the Lord’s Supper he holds out his body to be enjoyed by us, and to nourish us unto eternal life?” Calvin insists that by faith, Christians are made members of Jesus’s fleshly human body, so at communion, we experience all the benefits of spiritual union with him. Christ took on flesh so that in his ascended state, he might be a channel of righteousness to the believer, pouring into him all that Christ’s human life accomplished. content_zh:
最近,我(和我的同龄人)经历了一些皈依天主教的教区人士. 当我和这些皈依者交谈时, 他们发现鼓励用耶稣的身体和血液来识别面包和葡萄酒。

我听到过这样的话:乔治牧师,我喜欢耶稣在谈论主的晚餐,他说:“谁吃我的肉喝我的血,谁在我体内,我就在他体内”(John 6:56)。 如果我每天把耶稣带入我的身体, 虽然这种现象似乎更频繁地发生,

多年前,我和一个男人一起 为我们市的另一位牧师服务 我之前从未见过这个人;我只知道他直到最近才成为一所改革后福音神学院的教授。 这个人在耶稣号召福音的大臣们时宣扬一个坚实的信息,我为此感谢他. 然后,第二天,我看到他接受电视采访。

正如他所解释的,我需要比传统更现实的, 所以在午餐期间,我会走进罗马天主教当地的教区, 并带上尤查里会。 比起教会教义的“与基督结合的谜团”, 于是我辞去神学院的职务,回到了罗马.

我可以和那些脱离改革后信仰并加入罗马天主教、东正教或天主教传统的人交谈。 一个类似的主题贯穿于所有这些方面:渴望一个比改革后对主的晚餐提供的看法更具有转型性、感官性的现实。 这种批评有道理吗?

约翰·卡尔文会如何回应这种批评:如果你遵循改革后的晚餐观, 有时候,为了实现圣经上忠实的神学,改革后的基督徒只谈论圣餐的内容。 我痛苦地意识到我在这方面的缺点。

这可能无意中驱使一些信徒在其他传统中寻求更“真实”的经验。 我们可以在辩论面包和葡萄酒的确切性质时陷入困境,并忘记提出更紧迫的问题: 今天这顿饭怎么能改变我? 让我们回顾加尔文关于圣餐的教义。

我们将会重新恢复对桌子的憧憬, 简言之,加尔文告诉我们,主的晚餐是精神成长的燃料,因此,我们每次都应该期待地来到餐桌旁。

Calvin在其对以弗所发表的评论中写道:“保罗说,我们是他[基督]肉体和骨头的成员。

难道我们不知道,在主的晚餐中,他伸出他的身体,让我们享受,并使我们获得永生吗? 加尔文坚持认为,根据信仰,基督徒是耶稣肉体上的身体的成员,因此在圣餐时,我们体验到与他精神结合的所有好处.

title: To Sustain Inner-City Church Plants, Adopt a Missionary Model
summary: To plant churches in these spaces, we need to think like missionaries.
summary_zh: 要在这些地方建造教堂，我们需要像传教士一样思考。
title_zh: 为了维持内城教会植物，采用传教士模式
content: In a conversation at church one Sunday, a pastor told a friend of mine, “Your friend should quit trying to plant churches in the inner city. It doesn’t happen because it can’t happen.” I was visiting this friend just before COVID-19 hit, speaking at a separate church about our ministry, New England Urban Church Planting. Our organization was new, and my sinful inclination was to think, Oh, you just wait and see! My friend was equally defensive. Yet this pastor was onto something: It rarely happens, and it is indeed hard. Why is church planting in our nation’s neglected inner cities so rare? Why are underserved urban communities overlooked by gospel-preaching churches? Stakeholders in our ministry have discussed these questions since 2009, leading to the organization’s founding in 2020. We’ve learned a lot in these years of full-time work as we’re growing this network of inner-city planters. The work is hard for two key reasons. Yet it’s possible. And it’s crucial. Christ has commanded us to make disciples of all nations (Matt. 28:19)—this includes in our own nation’s inner cities. To plant churches in these spaces, we need to think like missionaries. Problem Unless you grew up in the inner city, serving there is a cross-cultural experience. This is the first reason church planting hard. Ruby Payne asks her readers if they can survive in poverty: Do you know how to keep your clothes from being stolen from a laundromat? Do you know how to move in half a day? Do you know how to keep your car from getting repossessed if you fall behind on payments? Discipling men and women in the inner city can be exasperating when they have a new burner phone frequently. Inner-city pastors need to know how to preach and how to administer Narcan. And behind all that is the sound of gunshots, fights, loud TVs, and the quiet exit of well-meaning suburban Christians who came to help but didn’t last long. Christ has commanded us to make disciples of all nations—this includes in our own nation’s inner cities. Evangelicalism often feels like it’s married to only one culture: suburbia. Postwar Americans migrated from our cities to set up homes and churches in the suburbs. In 1940, 15 percent of Americans lived in the suburbs. By 2000, that number was 50 percent. Evangelicals were a disproportionately high percentage of those who made the move. As this happened, Brian Miller argues , the values of suburbia melded with and shaped the values of evangelicalism. Churches in impoverished neighborhoods are rarely financially self-sustaining—the second challenge. Even if a pastor disciples his church toward generosity, being generous with a poverty-level income won’t pay the bills. So pastors who serve in these places get beaten down by serving a needy congregation while holding two other jobs “on the side.” It’s unsustainable. We don’t believe the answer for inner-city pastors should be a bi- or trivocational life. Solution The solution to these two challenges is within reach: the model of a supported foreign missionary. Since the late 18th century, the church has been training and sustaining men and women for gospel work in unfamiliar places, where they cannot expect the financial support of locals. This training-and-supporting model should be applied to inner-city church planting. The change we need has four aspects. The first is a change of heart. We need gospel-saturated hearts that understand that all people are impoverished by sin. Those living in a homeless encampment share the same fundamental condition as the wealthy suburbanite. Filled with gospel grace, we can move toward the poor because we’re more alike at heart than we are different. Our hearts must be shaped by the reality of Christ’s initiative to leave the riches of heaven for us, to become poor for us, that we might become rich (2 Cor. 8:9). Second, we need to believe that God’s heart is particularly inclined toward the overlooked (Ps. 72:12–14) and toward those generous toward them (Prov. 14:

title: Report Cards on Your Actions Won’t Fix Your Heart
summary: From GLP-1s to political reposts to mindfulness streaks, we’re all keeping score. Jesus says you can’t know who you are until you look at your heart.
summary_zh: 从GLP-1到政治转发，再到正念条纹，我们都在记分。耶稣说，除非你看看自己的内心，否则你无法知道自己是谁。
title_zh: 关于您行动的报告卡片无法修复您的心脏
content: Who am I? All cultures, human philosophies, and religious systems try to answer this question in a way that leads to a meaningful life. We want to find in them a path that allows us to say, “Who am I? I’m a good person. I’m someone who is living a good and right life.” What paths toward goodness and righteousness are being offered today? They’re as vast and varied as ever. One popular path is to optimize your life via medical improvements, ranging from plastic surgery to GLP-1s. The more you can “ humanmaxx ” your body to look healthier and be stronger, the more likely you’ll be considered an ideal human being—a good person to hire, to be friends with, to date or marry. Political engagement is another common path. Your goodness is determined by how connected you are to particular political movements. You can feel like you’re a good person when you make sure you quickly like and repost all Zohran Mamdani’s videos. Or alternatively, you’ll be affirmed as a good person by how aggressively you go after or insult people who like Mamdani. Paths our culture offers to the good life are often combined. Your sense of how good a person you are is measured by a mixture of how long you’ve engaged in therapy, how many hours you volunteer at your children’s school, and how long your streak is on your mindfulness app. Tara Isabella Burton, in her book Strange Rites: New Religions for a Godless World , argues that people have formed their own religious systems by drawing from various religions and philosophies. People have become “creators of their own bespoke religions, mixing and matching spiritual and aesthetic and experiential and philosophical traditions.” We’re doing a DIY project, grabbing and piecing together whatever’s around us, hoping we can come up with something to help us in our journey. So, what path does Christianity offer to assure us we’re living a good and righteous life? Keeping Score The Christian approach is to address what the Bible calls the heart. The heart is the Bible’s shorthand term for describing the part of you that drives and motivates you, what dictates your thoughts and emotions. Christianity starts with the heart because this is the only real way by which you can determine who you are and what needs to change. We see the contrast between the religious and cultural approach and the Christian approach in Jesus’s interaction with the Pharisees in Matthew 15:1–20. The Pharisees confront Jesus to ask him why his disciples don’t wash their hands before eating. Handwashing before meals was one of the many religious rules the Pharisees had developed, practiced, and called others to practice. For the Pharisees, the best answer to the question “Who am I?” was based on how well they followed their set standards. If a person kept the standard and had a life that could be observed to follow all the rules, then that person could definitively say to themselves and those around them, “I’m a good person who is living a good and right life.” Jesus’s story about the Pharisee in Luke 18:9–14 is another example. The Pharisee intently notes in his prayer how he, unlike the tax collector praying next to him, fasts twice a week and always gives the full tithe. Jesus describes the Pharisees in Matthew 6 as people who make sure their regular prayers can be seen and affirmed by all. The Pharisees weren’t alone in this approach. Greco-Roman religion had its own rules and standards to follow. Its gods demanded rituals, sacrifices, and festivals to appease and honor them. Performed rightly, they’d result in people securing the blessing they needed from the gods, thus assuring them their lives were good and righteous. Jesus, however, reframes the Pharisees’ questioning by showing that their approach doesn’t go far enough. Right living and human flourishing demands more than one’s outward actions. It requires harder interior examination. And that means looking at the heart. Jesus says, “What comes out of the mouth proceeds from the heart” (
content_zh:

title: Building a Workplace Where People Flourish (with Landon Hobson)
summary: What happens when a seminary-trained economist takes over a pet-products plant? Landon Hobson, CEO of Cosmos Corporation, shares how paid mission days, a book club, and a ‘make the coffee’ ethic help ordinary workers flourish.
summary_zh: 当受过神学院培训的经济学家接管宠物产品工厂时会发生什么？ Cosmos Corporation首席执行官兰登·霍布森（ Landon Hobson ）分享了带薪传教日、读书俱乐部和“制作咖啡”伦理如何帮助普通工人蓬勃发展。
title_zh: 打造让人们茁壮成长的工作场所（与Landon Hobson一起）
content: Landon Hobson is the CEO of Cosmos Corporation, a family business outside St. Louis that makes pet care and household cleaning products sold in 70 countries. With degrees in theology and economics, Landon never expected to run a 250,000-square-foot manufacturing plant—until his father-in-law asked him to take over the company, and he sensed that God had been preparing him for exactly that. Landon describes how his faith shapes Cosmos’s culture: tuition support for any degree an employee wants to pursue, a “Better Book Club” that pays people to read, five paid mission days a year, and a core value of being “willing to make the coffee” for the person behind you. He answers hard questions about whether making dog shampoo really matters to God, and he speaks candidly about the hard years—supply chain disruptions, a drop in sales, and layoffs of people he cared about. He also explains why CEOs need pastors who aren’t passive, and what he has gained from a group of believing business leaders who share the same struggles. Resources Mentioned: To Change the World by James Davison Hunter Every Good Endeavor by Timothy Keller A Public Faith by Miroslav Volf Work in the Spirit by Miroslav Volf

兰登·霍布森(Landon Hobson)是宇宙公司(Cosmos Corporation)的首席执行官,该公司是圣路易斯以外的一家企业,在70个国家销售宠物护理和家庭清洁产品. 凭借神学和经济学的学位,兰登从未预期会经营25万平方英尺的制造厂——直到岳父要求他接管公司,他感到上帝一直在为他做好完全这样的准备.

title: The Missing Piece in John Mark Comer’s Quiet Time
summary: ‘Into the Quiet’ effectively critiques the ills of our hectic cultural moment, but it also promotes a spirituality that could quickly become disconnected from Scripture.
summary_zh: “进入宁静”有效地批评了我们忙碌的文化时刻的弊端，但它也促进了一种可能很快与圣经脱节的灵性。
title_zh: 约翰·马克·科默安静时光中缺失的部分
content: According to a recent Pew Research study, more than half of U.S. adults report spending too much time on their smartphones. Even those who acknowledge the negative effects of smartphone addiction find it incredibly difficult to cut back. Excessive screen time isn’t just harming our productivity and connection with other people; it also makes practicing spiritual disciplines more challenging. In his latest book, Into the Quiet: Following Jesus in a World of Noise , John Mark Comer argues that “nurturing a practice of solitude, silence, and stillness is utterly indispensable to a flourishing spiritual life” (26). This timely book addresses important issues in a lively, engaging, and accessible manner. And though the staccato prose style sometimes borders on gimmicky, it’s never dull. Comer dons three hats, appearing as technoskeptic, therapist, and mystic. I responded differently to each: cheering the first, querying the second, and rejecting the third. Into the Quiet effectively critiques the ills of our hectic cultural moment, but it also makes questionable claims about the spiritual value of silence and promotes a spirituality that could quickly become disconnected from Scripture. Comer as Technoskeptic Comer’s consistent message is that readers need to intentionally disconnect from an increasingly noisy world. By “noise,” he means both literal sounds and the ever-present flood of distraction enabled by digital devices. The result is that “it is now possible to go through our entire lives and never be alone ” (18, emphasis original). Channeling secular authors like Jonathan Haidt and Johann Hari, Comer argues that constant noise threatens our well-being, whether we’re religious or not. But this dynamic is especially harmful for Christians. “Are we really surprised that . . . when we sit down to pray, we can barely even pay attention?” he asks (20). Our always-on lives differ greatly from the example of Jesus, who models a strategy of “retreat and return” (30). He ministers to the crowds and then withdraws to solitary places to pray (e.g., Matt. 14:23). This is the book’s strongest material, a timely warning with which I wholeheartedly agree. Comer as Therapist But then Comer moves in another direction. He advances therapeutic claims that may be helpful to some people but that aren’t clearly grounded in Scripture. According to Comer, solitude forces a confrontation with pain that serves an essential psychological purpose: All of this stuff is in you . . . leaking out like toxic pollution into the water supply of your relational world . . . it’s asking to be dealt with. To be given a moment to speak, say its piece. To be healed. Released. (85) While the imprecatory psalms and the psalms of lament certainly model honest prayer before the Lord, and self-examination is clearly a biblical imperative, Comer’s specific claims seem more informed by extrabiblical therapeutic practices than by Scripture itself. Is it actually true that “naming our feelings out loud allows our bodies to process and discharge pain without it getting lodged in our cores” (100)? That doesn’t sound like Scripture. According to Comer, solitude forces a confrontation with pain that serves an essential psychological purpose. The primary biblical support he gives for the practice of naming feelings to discharge pain is Jesus’s prayer in the garden of Gethsemane, an incident that provides the “template” for “the moments of our own Golgothas” (101). The problem is that Jesus in the garden isn’t surfacing old “toxic pollution” from “the water supply of [his] relational world” with an eye toward therapeutic healing (85). He’s facing an imminent crisis and asking the Father for either deliverance from or strength to face the trial set before him. Whatever the value of surfacing past trauma, Gethsemane doesn’t establish Comer’s claims on that point. 来者会戴三顶帽子 以技术怀疑者、治疗师和神秘主义者的身份出现 我对每一个都作出了不同的反应:欢呼第一个,询问第二个,拒绝第三个.

静悄悄地有效地批评了我们繁忙的文化时刻的弊端,但也提出了关于静悄悄的精神价值的令人怀疑的主张,并提倡一种精神性,这种精神性可能会很快脱离圣经. 读者需要有意与日益吵闹的世界断绝联系。

他所说的“噪音”既指文字上的声响,又指数字设备所引发的无时无刻不在的分散注意力。 其结果是,“现在有可能经历我们的整个生活,从不孤独......”(18,强调原文)。 comer指出, 不断的噪音威胁着我们的福祉, 无论我们是否信奉宗教。

但这种动态对基督徒特别有害. “当我们坐下来祷告时,我们甚至几乎不能注意,我们真的感到惊讶吗?” 我们始终不渝的生活与耶稣的榜样大不相同,耶稣树立了“遣返和返回”战略(30)。 他向人群派遣大臣,然后撤往单独地点祈祷(如马特14:23).

这是这本书最强的材料, 来者作为治疗师, 但随后,来者向另一个方向移动。 他提出治疗性要求,

据Comer说,孤独迫使与痛苦的对峙为基本的心理目的服务: 所有这些东西都在你体内, 渗出像有毒污染一样, 渗入你关系世界的水供应中, 得到时间说话,说说它的片段。 以被疗之. 释之.

(85) 虽然圣诗和哀叹的圣诗无疑是上帝面前的模范诚实祷告,而且自我检查显然是圣经的必经之义,但比起《圣经》本身,考美尔的具体主张似乎更能从圣经外的治疗做法中得到启发。

事实上,“大声点出我们的感情,使我们的身体能够处理和释放痛苦,而不将痛苦放在我们的核心中”(100)。 这听起来不像圣经。 据Comer说,孤独迫使一种与痛苦的对抗,这为基本的心理目的服务.

耶稣在Gethsemane的花园里祈祷,这是他为“我们自己的Golgothas(101)时刻”提供“时代”的主要圣经支持。 问题在于花园里的耶稣并没有从“关系世界的供水”中冒出老“有毒污染”,

他正面临迫在眉睫的危机, Gethsemane并没有证明Comer对此的主张。 来者如神秘 对于跟随Comer的作品的人来说,这不会令人惊讶,但他也强调一种神秘的形式.
author: Matthew Bingham

title: What Does It Mean to Be Human?: 12 Theses Answer a Pressing Question
summary: Learning about a Christian theological anthropology is no mere academic exercise. It gets to the heart of who we are, explains our daily experience, and pushes us toward the love of neighbor and the common good.
summary_zh: 学习基督教神学人类学不仅仅是学术练习。它触及我们的核心，解释我们的日常经历，并推动我们朝着爱邻居和公共利益的方向前进。
title_zh: 做人意味着什么？ ： 12篇论文回答了一个紧迫的问题
content: No question today is more pertinent than this: What does it mean to be human? With declining belief in God and rising secularization come renewed debates concerning human nature. Culture now seems to hold to two contradictory beliefs: Either that we’re entirely material beings, meaningless clumps of matter in an endless void; or that we’re sovereign masters who determine our own meaning, with an internal sense of who we are that we dare not defy. It’s no surprise that rejections of God lead to confusion concerning the image of God and the biblical teaching that we’re humbly related to this material cosmos and yet dignified as the crown of creation. With the advent of artificial intelligence and ongoing debates about race, gender, and sexuality, it’s all the more important to be clear about what we are and who we’re made to be. Learning about a Christian theological anthropology is no mere academic exercise. It gets to the heart of who we are, explains our daily experience, and pushes us toward the love of neighbor and the common good. A Christian theological anthropology gets to the heart of who we are and pushes us toward the love of neighbor and the common good. In my book, For Us and for Our Salvation , I seek to address these issues by providing a biblical, theological, and practical introduction to the doctrines of humanity and sin. In this article, I present 12 theses that summarize a biblical and Reformed-catholic theological anthropology that I explain throughout the book. These 12 theses, I hope, can ground us as we stand in culture’s ever-changing landscape. 1. All human beings are made in the image of the triune God and are thus called to represent, enjoy, and glorify God forever. God creates each individual according to his image. The first-person plural in Genesis 1:26 indicates that the whole triune God is the archetype for the human being, for each person of the Trinity shares a singular divine substance (see also Col. 1:15–17). Humans are created as representatives of God and are thus religious creatures made to have communion with their Origin. Therefore, each human being as such is created good, with dignity and agency. Our religiosity, corrupted by the fall, doesn’t lead us to cease being religious but rather causes us to elevate and idolize one aspect of creation over others, as we prefer the creature over the Creator (Rom. 1:18–23). We refuse to acknowledge God as the end for which we were made, and we seek enjoyment in other things—we idolize good, created reality and render it ultimate. 2. The doctrine of the image of God entails both ontological and ethical affirmations. God creates humans as embodied souls with intellectual and volitional capacities, and he calls humans to represent him by a proper exercise of those faculties in righteousness, holiness, and true knowledge. Human beings are endowed with capacities for wisdom and righteousness. A twofold metaphysical concept is important here: act and potency. Potency refers to the natural power that distinguishes a particular kind of thing from other kinds, and act refers to the exercise of that power. Humans, for instance, are the kinds of beings endowed with the potency to think rationally, but the actualization of those potencies is a distinct matter. Edward Feser clarifies , In arguing for the existence of active potencies or causal powers, Scholastic writers emphasize the point that a cause is not always bringing about its characteristic effect. . . . My power to write must therefore be distinguished from this or that actual, particular action of writing, as a standing precondition of the latter. Infants or those in a comatose state due to some serious injury, therefore, continue to be image-bearers, even while the potency for wisdom or will isn’t actualized in any way. Similarly, those who are cognitively impaired still have the potency or essential capacity of reason and volition even though it manifests differently than in others, and even if th
content_zh:
今天的问题莫过于: 何谓为人. 随着对上帝信仰的下降和世俗化的不断加深,关于人性的辩论又再度出现。 文化现在似乎持有两种相互矛盾的信念: 要么我们完全是物质生物,

或者我们是决定自己意义的主权主人, 对上帝的拒绝导致对上帝形象和圣经教义的困惑, 即我们与这个物质宇宙有着神圣的关系,

随着人工智能的出现和关于种族、性别和性问题的持续辩论的到来,更需要弄清楚我们是什么人,我们是谁。 学习基督教神学人类学不仅仅是学术实践. 它触及我们是谁的心脏, 解释我们的日常经历, 并把我们推向邻居的爱和共同利益。

一个基督教神学人类学 得到了我们的心脏 我们推向邻居的爱和共同利益。 在我《为了我们和我们的救世主》一书中,我试图通过提供一本圣经、神学和关于人类和罪恶理论的实际介绍来解决这些问题。

在这篇文章中,我提出了12篇论文,总结了一本圣经和改革天主教神学人类学,我在整个书中都对此作了解释. 我希望这12篇论文能让我们在文化不断变化的地貌中落脚。 1. 所有的人都是以三月神的形象塑造的,因此被召唤来代表、享受和永远颂扬上帝。

上帝根据他的形象创造每个人。 创世纪1:26中的第一人称复数表示,整个三角神是人类的原型,对于三位一体的每个人来说,都有一个独特的神性物质(另见1:15-17). 人类是作为上帝的代表而创造的,因此是宗教的生物,被赋予与他们的起源有共性.

因此,每个人都是善良、有尊严和有作用的。 我们的信仰被堕落所腐蚀, 并不导致我们不再信奉宗教,

我们拒绝承认真主是我们的末日,我们寻求享受,我们崇拜善神,创造现实,使它达到极点。 2. 关于上帝形象的理论包括本体论和伦理论。

上帝以智慧和意志能力创造人性,他号召人通过正确行使正义、圣洁和真正知识的才能来代表他。 人类拥有智慧和正义的能力。 这里有两个元概念很重要:行为和效力。

强力(potency)是指将某种特定事物与其他类型区分开来的自然力量,行为是指行使这种力量. 例如,人类是具有理性思考能力的生物,但是,这些能力的实现是一个独特的问题。

Edward Feser澄清说,在主张存在主动的力量或因果力量时,学术作家强调一个原因并不总是能产生其特征效应。  . 因此,我的写作能力必须与这种或那种实际的、特别的写作行动区分开来,作为后者的长期先决条件。

因此,婴儿或因严重伤害而处于昏迷状态的人继续是形象的持有者,即使智慧或意志的力量根本没有实现。 同样,那些在认知上受损的人仍然具有理智和意志的能力或基本能力,尽管这种能力的表现与其他人不同,而且即使存在这种能力。

title: Your Church May Know Less Bible Than You Think (And What to Do About It)
summary: A new survey indicates Christians have succumbed to the general literacy crisis of the culture. The ‘people of the Book’ don’t read it.
summary_zh: 一项新的调查显示，基督徒已经屈服于该文化的普遍识字危机。“书中的人”不读它。
title_zh: 你的教会可能知道的圣经比你想象的要少（以及该怎么做）
content: In November 1900, Mark Twain delivered a speech titled “The Disappearance of Literature” to the students at Connecticut Wesleyan University. With signature slyness, he told them , “I don’t believe any of you have ever read Paradise Lost , and you don’t want to. That’s something that you just want to take on trust. It’s . . . the definition of a classic—something that everybody wants to have read and nobody wants to read.” Twain was noting the beginning of the illiteracy rockslide that we now witness as an avalanche. The statistics we see in the age of smartphones and social media bear out our eroded literacy: In 2003, average Americans older than age 15 read 21.9 minutes on a given day. By 2010, the number had dropped to 18.3 minutes, and in 2025, it had sunk to 16.2 minutes a day. Imagine how ChatGPT will gut that number even further in the next few years. America is moving rapidly into a postliterate reality, a sort of new Dark Ages, one in which we consume information in images and sound bites, all predigested for us by others. Consider the implications for a system of belief whose transmission from one generation to the next is staked on a book. Christian Literacy Crisis A new survey from Lifeway Research throws into stark relief the chasm between Christian commitment to and knowledge of the Bible. More than 2,000 Christians who attend church in a typical month were surveyed across eight categories of Bible knowledge: major people, passages, events, divisions of Scripture, and more. The researchers designed questions around what would be typically well known rather than obscure. Two out of three respondents scored less than 60, a failing grade. Fifty-five percent could not correctly name the first king of Israel. Only 11 percent could correctly order four major Old Testament events, and only 27 percent could correctly order four major New Testament events. Forty-four percent failed to identify the book of Mark as belonging to the Gospels. Two out of three respondents wrongly believed Hezekiah was a book of the Bible, and 44 percent believed the Gospel of Thomas was as well. Christians have succumbed to the general literacy crisis of the culture. The “people of the Book” don’t read it. The Bible itself, the classic of all classics, has apparently become a book that every Christian wants to have read, and few Christians want to read. If we do read to sustain our faith, we’re more likely to read books about the Bible than the Bible itself. We may consume sermons or podcasts or use devotional resources that cherry-pick verses to give us a positive emotion in 10 minutes or less, but largely, we’ve become curators of other people’s opinions about a book we don’t read ourselves. Failure of Discipleship I believe these results show a failure of discipleship strategies, one with massive implications: We cannot pass along to someone else what we ourselves don’t know. How can the church fulfill the Great Commission if it’s incapable of teaching others to observe everything Jesus commanded? The numbers show we haven’t taught even the basics. If the church were a local public school responsible for teaching basic math and reading, we would receive a failing grade and face funding sanctions. The ‘people of the Book’ don’t read it. Yet, according to a 2024 Lifeway Research survey of 2,620 Protestant pastors, 52 percent are satisfied with the state of discipleship and spiritual formation in their churches. Twenty-nine percent report that they regularly evaluate discipleship progress among their congregations. When asked their first priority in discipleship, the largest number responded that it be “biblical knowledge focused.” And in response to the question “What approaches does your church specifically use to disciple and encourage the spiritual development of adults in your congregation?” 89 percent responded the sermon, the top answer by a 20-point gap, with adult Sunday school listed second. title: Does Christianity Make Sense? On God, Evil, and the Ache (with Gavin Ortlund)
summary: Gavin Ortlund joins Collin Hansen to discuss apologetics and why Christianity makes sense.
summary_zh: 加文·奥特伦德（ Gavin Ortlund ）与科林·汉森（ Collin Hansen ）一起讨论了护教学以及基督教为什么有意义。
title_zh: 基督教有意义吗？论上帝、邪恶和痛苦（与Gavin Ortlund合作）
content: Not long ago, my son asked me about all the people King David killed in 2 Samuel 8. We’ve been reading through that book during family devotions before bed. He’s right to be disturbed. So we had a conversation about why he’s unnerved, how we develop moral instincts, and how we’d respond to someone who rejects God because of these and similar accounts in the Old Testament. We did apologetics together. As he gets a little older, I’ll point him toward the YouTube channel of my friend Gavin Ortlund, who does an excellent job of answering many hard questions about Christianity and the Bible. Then, a few years later, I’ll point him to Gavin’s books, including his latest, Why Christianity Makes Sense: A Book About Jesus, the Mysteries of the World, and the Longings in Your Heart (Zondervan Reflective). He’s back on Gospelbound to discuss all things apologetics, from the multiverse, to slavery, to morality as merely a taste for sugar, to winning the lottery 10 billion times in a row. title: I Was a Justice Warrior. I Needed the Whole Gospel. You Do Too.
summary: Most Christians today see these two gospel aspects as part of the same biblical pie. But we often fail to see them as necessarily intertwined.
summary_zh: 今天，大多数基督徒将这两个福音方面视为同一个圣经馅饼的一部分。但我们往往看不到它们必然交织在一起。
title_zh: 我是一名正义战士。我需要完整的福音。你也是。
content: From 2016 to 2018, I was a social media justice warrior. I spent my time on Facebook and Twitter confronting the powerful and comfortable, championing justice issues, and fighting for racial and political reconciliation. If you read my posts, you might not have guessed that I grew up in a conservative Christian home nestled in suburbia, or that I spent every day of my education, starting at age 4, in Christian schools. In my upbringing, I learned the rich depths of the Christian faith. I surrendered my life to Jesus, and I learned that Jesus came to seek to save the lost. Yet that evangelistically oriented world of my youth was intentionally sanitized and separated from the painful realities of poverty and injustice just 10 minutes down the road. When I discovered this disparity, I became a justice warrior online. And while that posture was certainly a reaction to my upbringing, I wasn’t being a hypocrite. My social media advocacy reflected my actual life. I’ve lived and worked in an underresourced neighborhood since 2001. During my first 15 years in the neighborhood, I grew burdened over the disconnect I saw between the conditions my neighbors faced daily and how many in the American church live. The political, racial, and socioeconomic divide between my church life and neighborhood gutted me. So when I went online, I was convinced I was sharing the true gospel. Yet that “gospel” I shared was merely centered on producing tangible results in the here and now, not on affecting eternity. What I needed instead was a holistic gospel, one that centers around both God’s kingdom mission and also his sacrificial death for sinners on the cross. Two Gospel Aspects I began to see two aspects in the biblical gospel. Let’s call them the gospel of the cross and the gospel of the kingdom . The gospel of the cross is the good news that Jesus Christ saves and adopts believers as his children through his substitutionary death and glorious resurrection. We’re all born alienated from God. In sin, we’re his enemies. In Christ, as we believe the good news, we’re reconciled to God (Rom. 5:6–10) and assured of eternal life with him (John 3:16). As Peter writes, “Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God” (1 Pet. 3:18). Moreover, the cross aspect of the gospel emphasizes that those entrusted with this message must share it with a lost and dying world (Matt. 28:18–20). The gospel of the cross must be heralded; it must be proclaimed. It is the priority. From this gospel flows every good gift. What I needed instead was a holistic gospel, one that centers around both God’s kingdom mission and also his sacrificial death for sinners on the cross. The gospel of the kingdom is the good news that God’s will for justice, goodness, and peace is already being unleashed. As God’s children, believers are invited to play a part in seeing that kingdom mission come to fruition. Jesus begins his ministry by preaching a message that proclaims “good news to the poor” and “liberty to the . . . oppressed” (Luke 4:18). He calls his hearers to repent, including from ways they’ve oppressed and neglected the poor (Matt. 3:2; 4:17). He specifically rebukes the Pharisees for neglecting “the weightier matters of the law: justice and mercy and faithfulness” (23:23). Paul, too, teaches that the gospel not only reunites us to God but also works justice by reconciling divided peoples to one another in the church. He writes, “For [Christ] himself is our peace, who has made us both [ethnic groups] one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility” (Eph. 2:14). We fulfill the law and live out the gospel’s kingdom implications through our identity as shalom -makers (Matt. 5:9). The kingdom aspect of the gospel equips us with a vision for pursuing God’s will “on earth as it is in heaven” (6:10), that is, for seeing all things made new (Rev. 21:5). 2016年至2018年,任社交媒体正义战士. 我花时间在脸书和推特上,

如果你读过我的文章, 你可能没有猜到 我成长在一个保守的基督教家庭 在郊区, 或者我每天的教育, 从4岁开始在基督教学校。 在我成长的过程中,我学会了基督教信仰的丰富深度. 我把自己的生命交给耶稣,我得知耶稣是来寻求拯救失落者.

然而,这个以福音为本的我青年世界被故意洗涤,并在仅仅10分钟之内就脱离了贫困和不公正的痛苦现实。 当我发现这种差距时,我成了在线上的正义战士。 虽然这种姿态无疑是对我的成长的反应, 我的社交媒体宣传反映了我的真实生活.

自2001年起, 在附近15年里, 我对邻居每天面临的状况 和美国教堂里有多少人的生活脱节感到负担沉重。 我的教会生活和邻居之间的政治、种族和社会经济鸿沟使我心碎。

所以当我上网时,我确信我分享了真正的福音。 然而,我所分享的“神灵”仅仅集中于在这里和现在产生实际结果,而不是影响永恒。 我所需要的是一个全方位的福音,它既围绕上帝的王国使命,也围绕着他为十字架上的罪人而牺牲的死亡。

我开始看到圣经福音中的两个方面。 让我们称之为十字架的福音和王国的福音。 十字架的福音是好消息,耶稣基督通过他的替代死亡和光荣的复活来拯救和接纳信徒作为自己的孩子. 我们天生都与上帝隔绝。 在罪恶中,我们是他的敌人。

在基督中,我们相信好消息,我们与上帝和解(5:6-10室),并保证与上帝永生(John 3:16). 正如彼得所写的那样,“基督也曾因罪恶而受苦,善人因不义者而受苦,以便他把我们带到上帝面前”(第3:18页)。

此外,福音的交叉方面强调,受委托传达这一信息的人必须与一个迷失和垂死的世界分享(Matt. 28:18-20)。 十字架的福音必须预告;必须宣布。 这是优先事项。 从这个福音中流传着每一个好礼物.

我所需要的是一个全方位的福音,它既围绕上帝的王国使命,也围绕着他为十字架上的罪人而牺牲的死亡。 王国的福音是好消息,上帝对正义、善良与和平的意志已经释放。 作为上帝的子孙,信徒们被邀请在确保王国使命取得成果方面发挥作用。

耶稣在部里首先发出一个信息,宣称“向穷人提供好消息”和“向......受压迫的人提供自由”(公爵4:18)。 他呼吁他的听众悔改,包括他们压迫和忽视穷人的方式(Matt. 3:2;4:17)。 他特别斥责法利赛人忽视“较重要的法律事项:正义、慈悲和忠诚”(23:23)。

保罗也教导道,福音不仅使我们与上帝团聚,而且通过在教会中调和分裂的人民来伸张正义。 他写道,“[基督]自己是我们的和平,他使我们两个[种族群 都成了和平,并用他的肉体打破了敌对的分隔墙”(Eph 2:14)。

我们履行法律,通过我们作为立法者的身份,活出福音的王国影响(马特:9)。 福音的王国方面为我们提供了追求上帝的旨意的愿景,即 " 在地上像在天上一样 " (6:10),即看到一切事物都变新(Rev.21:5)。 王国的福音 必须通过神圣的 行动而存在

title: Lessons from Lloyd-Jones on Preaching and Politics
summary: Here are three lessons we can learn from Martyn Lloyd-Jones’s ministry in a time of political crisis.
summary_zh: 在政治危机时期，我们可以从马丁·劳埃德-琼斯（ Martyn Lloyd-Jones ）的事工中学到三个教训。
title_zh: 劳埃德-琼斯关于讲道和政治的教训
content: “I was never worried for a second about a man like Hitler.” This isn’t the statement of a madman or of someone privileged enough to be removed from the horrors of the war. These are the words of a pastor who was under immediate threat from the Nazi leader and who’d put on the full armor of God and prepared for battle. Adolf Hitler invaded Poland on September 1, 1939; the very next day, Martyn Lloyd-Jones was installed as an associate pastor at Westminster Chapel in London, where he would faithfully preach for the next 30 years. One year after the preacher took the pulpit, Hitler began his bombing campaign over London. Of the roughly 700 churches in the area, 624 were damaged by the bombings and 91 were totally destroyed. To the surprise of many, Westminster Chapel, one of London’s largest churches at the time, wasn’t destroyed in the bombing blitz. Iain Murray, in his classic biography on Lloyd-Jones , writes about one Sunday morning when a bomb hit close to the Chapel right in the middle of Lloyd-Jones’s Lord’s Day prayer. The bomb shook the entire building, and plaster and dust fell down on the congregation, including on “the Doctor,” as Lloyd-Jones was known. After a pause, Lloyd-Jones simply continued his prayer and the service went forward unimpeded. Lloyd-Jones offers a needed corrective to our politically anxious times. Some Christians resort to despair, while others attempt revolution. What we need is a political theology that still preaches Christ when the bombs go off. Here are three lessons we can learn from Lloyd-Jones’s ministry in a time of political crisis. Refuse Saul’s Armour When it became apparent that England was entering the war, Lloyd-Jones sent his wife and their two children back to Wales and away from the city, not knowing what would become of it. In a brief and urgent correspondence to his wife, he writes , “Leave yourself and me too, and everything in God’s hand and you will find peace and rest.” With bombs flying overhead, many in the church were calling for a revolution, but Lloyd-Jones was calling for prayer. With bombs flying overhead, many in the church were calling for a revolution, but Lloyd-Jones was calling for prayer. Because of fear and panic, many began to abandon the weapons of the church and replace them with the weapons of the state. But Lloyd-Jones refused to blur the lines. When the war was at its worst and his congregation had been reduced to few because of death and displacement, he remained resolute in affirming 2 Corinthians 10:4: “The weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds” (KJV). Lloyd-Jones refused to allow revolutionary alliances and tactics to infiltrate the church: Alas, far too often the church has tried to meet the world and its persecuting power with like weapons to those employed by the enemy. She has made alliances with the state and she has tried to strengthen herself in a material sense. She has been slow to discover what David discovered long ago in his fight with Goliath, that she cannot fight in the armour of Saul, but must ever use her own weapons with which she is familiar and with which she is meant to use. Lloyd-Jones saw a parallel between those in Saul’s armory who were looking to outfit David for battle with new calls from within the church to align herself with the state. Like David’s pitiful sling, prayer may appear in the world’s eyes woefully insufficient weaponry against fascism. But God’s weapons are greater than the weapons of men. Reject the Partisan Gospel Lloyd-Jones saw that the church was particularly vulnerable to political idolatry when fear had gripped the people. Like the Israelites shaking at the sight of Goliath, we often feel the only reasonable response is to find our own “strong man” to fight our battles. Throughout the church’s history, we’ve often turned to national politics. In a talk titled “ Living in Revolutionary Times ,” Lloyd-Jones rebukes the evangelicals of his day, w

第二天,马丁·劳埃德-琼斯 被安置在伦敦的威斯敏斯特礼拜堂做副牧师 他将在接下来的30年里忠实地传教 传教士攻下弹坑一年后,希特勒开始对伦敦的轰炸战役. 在该地区约700座教堂中,有624座被炸毁,91座被完全摧毁。

在与他妻子的简短和紧急的通信中,他写道:"离开你和我,以及上帝手中的一切,你会得到安宁和安息。 随着炸弹在高空飞翔,教堂里许多人呼吁革命,但劳埃德-琼斯呼吁祈祷. 随着炸弹在高空飞翔,教堂里许多人呼吁革命,但劳埃德-琼斯呼吁祈祷.

由于恐惧和恐慌,许多人开始放弃教会的武器,代之以国家的武器. 但劳埃德-琼斯拒绝模糊界限.

当战争处于最糟糕的状态,他的集会由于死亡和流离失所而减少到极少数时,他仍然坚决申明2科林斯人10:4:“我们战争的武器不是肉体的,而是通过上帝而强大的力量来拉倒坚固的控制力”(KJV)。

劳埃德-琼斯拒绝让革命联盟和战术渗透到教会中:唉,教会经常试图用类似武器来对付世界及其迫害敌人者的力量. 她与国家结盟,并试图在物质上加强自己。

她一直缓慢地发现大卫很久以前在与高丽的战斗中发现的东西,即她不能在索尔的盔甲中作战,但必须永远使用自己熟悉的,本意使用的武器.

劳埃德-琼斯在索尔的军械库里看到了一个相似之处, 与大卫的悲哀一样,祈祷可能出现在世界的眼中,令人悲哀的是,反对法西斯主义的武器不足。 但上帝的武器比人的武器还要大

title: Develop Healthy Tech Habits with Your Teen
summary: ‘Scroll Less, Live More’ helps teens and parents develop the tech skills they need to live a life rooted in reality and steeped in wisdom.
summary_zh: “少滚动，多活”可以帮助青少年和家长培养他们所需的技术技能，从而过上扎根于现实、充满智慧的生活。
title_zh: 与青少年一起养成健康的科技习惯
content: Each Sunday night at youth group, our time of worship through singing is followed by a short sermon then small-group discussion. The high school kids in the group I lead know the routine. Before we open the Scriptures, we pull our chairs into a circle. Then we take out our phones and stack them in a pile on the floor in the middle of the ring. We won’t touch those screens again until the Bible-study hour is done. The phone stack is a simple habit. But it’s helped the students in our group pay closer attention to both one another and the Bible text. In his practical new book, Scroll Less, Live More: 10 Healthy Tech Habits for Teens , Samuel James commends a number of similar practices. His goal is to give teenagers “a vivid picture of what it looks like to apply [biblical] wisdom to technology usage in today’s digital age” (155). James recognizes that simple, repeatable practices can help young people resist the foolishness today’s tech promotes so they can instead grow in the fear of the Lord. Great Power, Great Responsibility Scroll Less, Live More builds on the foundation James laid in his previous book for adults, Digital Liturgies: Rediscovering Christian Wisdom in an Online Age . One of his main premises is that technology isn’t neutral. Rather, it’s a powerful force that “shapes and influences us in ways we aren’t always aware of” (30). One way tech changes us is by changing our expectations. To illustrate this truth, James points to tech invented in the 19th century: Before the telephone . . . people just accepted that if they weren’t in the same room as somebody, they couldn’t communicate with that person in the moment. After the telephone was introduced, being able to communicate with someone in a different place at any time became not only possible but also important. (125) Similarly, 21st-century tech such as generative AI brings with it both new possibilities and greater expectations: “AI’s capability to produce an amazing variety of work and art with very little direct human involvement creates an expectation that using it regularly for these purposes is normal” (127). The more we off-load our creativity and effort to it, the more we believe we should do so. One way tech changes us is by changing our expectations. Digital technology changes us in other ways too. James draws on the work of tech realists such as Neil Postman , Nicholas Carr , and Marshall McLuhan , but he makes their perspective accessible for adolescents. James repeatedly shows young people how poor digital habits affect their cognition, emotions, and relationships. Living on a phone will slow down thinking, leaving teens feeling anxious, or even angry, amid daily interactions that then become more awkward and strained. Way of Wisdom: Guard Your Heart How do we help young people avoid this path? James gives teens some practical encouragements, telling them to charge their phones somewhere other than in their bedrooms overnight. He also provides a list self-examination questions to help them grow in self-awareness and he appeals to family rules such as only using devices in open areas of the home. But ultimately, James is convinced that using technology well involves more than simply following a list of dos and don’ts. He writes, We don’t need a huge list of rules that will have to be updated every time Apple releases a new phone or a new social media app; we need something that will help us determine how to use technology well in any circumstance. We need wisdom. (16–17) Proverbs says, “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, and the knowledge of the Holy One is insight” (9:10). James is clear that growing in wisdom and the knowledge of the Lord requires more than adjusting one’s screen-time settings; it takes guarding one’s heart. James encourages teens to think of their hearts as a palace where a king or queen lives. He says, “In any royal palace, you’re sure to find soldiers keeping watch over who and what has access to the very importa

每个星期天晚上,在青年团体,我们通过唱歌进行礼拜的时间,接着是简短的布道,然后是小组讨论。 我带领的高中生们都懂规矩 在打开"圣经"前,把椅子拉入一圈. 然后我们拿出我们的电话 把它们堆在地上 戒指中间。

我们不会再碰那些屏幕, 电话堆是一个简单的习惯。 这帮助了我们团体的学生更密切地关注彼此和圣经文本。 在他实用的新书"Scroll Less"(Scroll Less, Live More: 10 Health Tech Habits for Teens)中,塞缪尔·詹姆斯称赞了一些类似的做法.

他的目标是让青少年 " 生动地了解在当今数字时代将[圣经上 智慧应用于技术应用的外表 " (155)。 詹姆斯认识到简单、可重复的做法可以帮助年轻人抵制当今技术推广的愚蠢,让他们在上帝的恐惧中成长。

Great Power, Great Responsibility Scroll Less, Live More 在他的前作中为成年人奠定的基础上, 科技并非中立。 而是一股强大的力量, “塑造并影响我们,

技术改变我们的方法之一是改变我们的期望。 为了说明这个事实,詹姆斯指出19世纪发明的技术: 在电话之前, 人们刚刚接受, 如果他们不和别人在同一间屋子里,

在电话引入后,能够随时与另一个地方的某个人通信不仅成为可能,而且非常重要.

(125) 同样地,21世纪的技术,如基因人工智能,也带来了新的可能性和更大的期望: " 人工智能在人类很少直接参与的情况下生产出惊人的作品和艺术的能力,使人们期望经常用于这些目的是正常的 " (127)。 我们越是放弃我们的创造力和努力,我们就越相信我们应该这样做。

技术改变我们的方法之一是改变我们的期望。 数字技术也以其他方式改变我们。 James借鉴了Neil Postman、Nicholas Carr、Marshall McLuhan等科技现实主义者的作品, 詹姆斯反复地向年轻人展示,不良的数字习惯如何影响他们的认知,情感和关系.

生活在电话里会减缓思考, 让青少年感到焦虑甚至愤怒, 智慧之道:守护你的心 我们如何帮助年轻人避免这条道路? 詹姆斯给青少年一些实际的鼓励,让他们在一夜之间在卧室以外的地方充电电话.

他还提供了一份自查问题清单,帮助他们提高自我意识,他呼吁遵守家庭规则,例如只在家庭的空地使用装置。 但最终,詹姆斯相信,使用良好的技术不仅仅涉及遵循一个做和不做的清单。

他写道, 我们不需要一连串的规则, 每次苹果公司发布新手机或新社交媒体应用时, 我们需要智慧。 (16-17) 普罗活佛说:"对耶和华的恐惧是智慧的开始,对圣者的知识是洞察力"(9:10).

詹姆斯明白,智慧和上帝的知识的不断增长,不仅需要调整一个人的屏幕时间设置,还需要守护一个人的心。 詹姆斯鼓励青少年将心想成一个国王或女王所居住的宫殿. 他说,“在任何皇家宫殿里,你肯定能找到士兵来监视谁和谁能进入这个宫殿。

content: Edited by John Hendryx in epub , .mobi & .pdf formats Since faith is infinitely beyond all the power of our unregenerated human nature, it is only God who can give the spiritual ears to hear and eyes to see the beauty of Christ in the gospel. God alone disarms the hostility of the sinner turning his heart of stone to a heart of flesh (2 Cor 4:4-6). It is God, the Holy Spirit, alone who gives illumination and understanding of His word that we might believe; It is God who raises us from the death of sin, who circumcises the heart; unplugs our ears; It is God alone who can give us a new sense, a spiritual capacity to behold the beauty and unsurpassed excellency of Jesus Christ. The apostle John recorded Jesus saying to Nicodemus that we naturally love darkness, hate the light and WILL NOT come into the light (John 3:19, 20). And since our hardened resistance to God is thus seated in our affections, only God, by His grace, can lovingly change, overcome and pacify our rebellious disposition. The natural man, apart from the quickening work of the Holy Spirit, will not come to Christ on his own since he is at enmity with God and cannot understand spiritual things (1 Cor 2:14). Shining a light into a blind man's eyes will not enable him to see, because eyesight first requires a set of healthy eyes.

title_zh: 系统神学二
content: by Louis Berkhof In ePub , .mobi and .pdf formats You may also download the separate Introductory Volume to Systematic Theology here. Professor Berkhof, who was the President of Calvin Seminary and professor of Systematic Theology at the same in the first half of the twentieth century, has given us an excellent compendium of Reformed theological thought in this hefty volume. The subject is treated in the classical style, moving through the Doctrines of God, Man in Relation to God, the Person and Work of Christ, the Application of the Work of Redemption, the Church and the Means of Grace, and the Last Things. For decades, Louis Berkhof’s Systematic Theology has remained one of the most important and widely-used systematic theologies. It provides the clearest and most succinct articulation of Reformed theology. From its first publication in 1932, Berkhof’s work was revised, reprinted, and translated into Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Spanish, and Portuguese, and it had become a standard theological text by 1950. It has gained near-universal use in seminaries and Bible colleges across the world, and is widely cited and used by pastors, theologians, and students of nearly all denominational affiliations.
content_zh: 由路易·伯克霍夫(Louis Berkhof)撰写 在ePub,.mobi和.pdf格式中 您也可以在此下载系统神学的单独入门卷 。 贝尔克霍夫教授曾于20世纪上半叶担任卡尔文神学院院长和系统神学教授,在本书中为我们提供了一份出色的改革神学思想简编. 主题以古典风格来对待,通过"上帝的理论","人与上帝的关系","基督的人与工作","救赎之作的应用","教会与恩赐的手段","最后的事情"等来进行. 数十年来,路易·伯克霍夫的"系统神学"仍然是最重要和被广泛应用的系统神学之一. 它为改革神学提供了最清楚和最简洁的阐述。 从1932年的首次出版起,伯克霍夫的作品被修改,再版,并被翻译成了中文,日文,韩文,西班牙文和葡萄牙文,到1950年已经成为标准的神学文本. 它在世界各地的神学院和圣经学院获得了近乎普遍的使用,并被牧师、神学家和几乎所有教派派别的学生广泛引用和使用。

content: by Thomas Manton in ePub , .mobi & .pdf formats SUCH is the divine matter and admirable order of the Lord’s Prayer, as became the eternal wisdom of God, that composed and dictated it to his disciples. In it are opened the fountains of all our regular petitions, and the arguments contained to encourage our hopes for obtaining them. In our addresses to men, our study is to conciliate their favourable audience; but God is most graciously inclined and ready to grant our requests, therefore we are directed to call upon him by the title of ‘Our Father in heaven,’ to assure us of his love and power, and thereby to excite our reverent attention, to raise our affections, to confirm our confidence in prayer. The supreme end of our desires is the glory of God, in conjunction with our own happiness: this is expressed in the two first petitions, that ‘his name may be hallowed,’ and ‘his kingdom come,’ that we may partake of its felicity. In order to this, our desires are directed for the means that are proper and effectual to accomplish it. And those are of two kinds — the good things that conduct us, and the removal of those evils that obstruct our happiness.

content: by Archibald Alexander In ePub , .mobi and .pdf formats On the basis of fifty years as a pastor, preacher and professor at Princeton Theological Seminary, Archibald Alexander (1772-1851) deals with the subjective work of the Holy Spirit in the heart in all its phases, from the new birth until final preparation for heaven. There are two kinds of religious knowledge which, though intimately connected as cause and effect, may nevertheless be distinguished. These are the knowledge of the truth as it is revealed in the Holy Scriptures; and the impression which that truth makes on the human mind when rightly apprehended. The first may be compared to the inscription or image on a seal, the other to the impression made by the seal on the wax. When that impression is clearly and distinctly made, we can understand, by contemplating it, the true inscription on the seal more satisfactorily, than by a direct view of the seal itself. Thus it is found that nothing tends more to confirm and elucidate the truths contained in the Word, than an inward experience of their efficacy on the heart. It cannot, therefore, be uninteresting to the Christian to have these effects, as they consist in the various views and affections of the mind, traced out and exhibited in their connection with the truth, and in their relation to each other.

content: "Although They Knew God ... They Suppressed the Truth..." The opportunities are wide open for Christians to speak with secular people these days, especially if you live in a metropolitan area. The average hipster you may meet in the medium to big sized city is a secularist who may listen to NPR, has a liberal, ecological, and/or anti-capitalist political ideology ... wears vintage clothing from a thrift store and consumes ethically. He or she often either rides a bike, uses public transportation or even may be driving a hybrid or bio-diesel vehicle. This person is deeply concerned with the ethical treatment of animals, is strongly against slavery, torture, racism and political oppression against women. In other words, he takes morality very seriously. Another characteristic of this individual is that he/she thinks Christianity is irrelevant at best. Since we deeply care about the eternal destinies of such individuals how should we go about reaching such a person with the gospel? Where would you start? Once of the more effective ways, I have found, is to remember that that your secular friend already knows God exists. He/she knows God exists and lives as if He does. In Romans chapter 1 Paul clearly teaches this about all people when he says, "For although they knew God" (verse 21) "...by their unrighteousness suppress the truth" (verse 18). But how can we demonstrate to your friends that they already believe in God, when intellectually they deny His existence? While there are many ways this could be done, I would like to suggest one way that I have found to be quite persuasive: The knowledge of God through their own morality.
content_zh: "虽然他们认识上帝... 这些天基督徒与世俗人士交谈的机会是广阔的,特别是如果你生活在一个都市地区. 在中等至大城市中,你可能遇到的平凡的嬉皮士是一个世俗主义者,他可能听从NPR,具有自由主义,生态主义和/或反资本主义的政治意识形态.穿着节俭店出产的古装并合乎道德地消费. 他或她往往要么骑自行车,使用公共交通,要么甚至可能驾驶混合或生物柴油车辆. 此人对动物的道德待遇深感关切,强烈反对奴役、酷刑、种族主义和对妇女的政治压迫。 换句话说,他非常重视道德。 这个人的另一个特征是,heshe认为基督教最多是无关紧要的. 既然我们深深地关心这些人的永恒命运,那么我们如何用福音去帮助这样一个人呢? 你从哪里开始? 我发现,最有效的方法之一 就是记住,你的世俗朋友已经知道上帝的存在。 他/她知道上帝的存在 并活得像他一样 在罗马人第一章中,保罗明确教导了这一点,他说:"虽然他们认识上帝"(第21节)"......以不义压制真理"(第18节). 但我们怎能向你的朋友证明,他们已经信仰了真主,而他们在理智上否认他的存在呢? 虽然有许多方法可以做到这一点,但我想建议一种方法,我认为它很有说服力: 以自德而知神.

title_zh: ‘年轻人，你看起来很悲惨’
content: I’m excited to tell you the story of how God used a simple verse, from a complicated passage, to change the life of a man named Charles Spurgeon. His story is for everyone, but it may have a special word to speak to a few groups in the room. One is laymen — that is, people who work for a living in normal jobs, outside of Christian ministry. People without a seminary education, people who aren’t pastors or have ministry jobs. We recognize that this series has profiled four men who were preachers. Now, there is an interesting flow to our series: - first, Saint Augustine, - then, Luther, who was an Augustinian monk, - then, John Bunyan, whose favorite book outside the Bible was Luther’s commentary on Galatians, - now, Charles Spurgeon, whose favorite book outside the Bible was Bunyan’s Pilgrim’s Progress. We’ve moved from one convert to another, each building in some way on the previous one, but a weakness of our series (in some sense) is that they all became preachers. And we don’t expect you all to become preachers; we’d like a few, but most will be laymen, and that’s good. Now, Spurgeon is known as “the Prince of Preachers.” But the hero, under God, in Spurgeon’s story is not Spurgeon, and not a trained, paid preacher, but a layman. So, Spurgeon’s story has a special word for laymen who are willing to open their mouths and say what they know about Jesus. Spurgeon’s story also has a special word for teens and young adults. Spurgeon came to faith at age fifteen, which in his day was far more like young adulthood. Still, his story offers a challenge to those who are no longer children and not yet established adults: teens, college students, grad students, even young professionals. Don’t let the world (or the church) lower your standards of what’s possible in being deeply converted and dedicated to Jesus — and how God can make his Son thrilling to a young soul. My prayer is that God might be pleased to give some their own engine. So often, parents, college workers, and pastors help young adults along and give them pushes. And then sometimes, God is pleased in the life of teenagers to give them their own engine, and they don’t need any more pushing. They say, “Get out of my way! I am going to follow Jesus. You can’t keep me from him and worship, my Bible, and prayer!” That’s what God did for Spurgeon at age fifteen — he gave him his own engine. And I pray he might be pleased to do that even here this morning. Spurgeon’s story speaks to one more group: those in the room who are willing to admit, “I’m here but I’m not saved.” For two thousand years, unsaved people have shown up at churches for all sorts of reasons. That’s Spurgeon’s story. He was searching. He was unsaved and in a church on a Sunday morning when God broke through. So, if you’d say this morning, “I haven’t settled the issue of my sin and rebellion against God,” or “I haven’t ‘been saved,’” or “if I died on the drive home today, I wouldn’t be at peace with my Maker,” this story has a special word for you. So, let me tell you about Charlie Spurgeon. His Early and Whole Life He was born in 1834, about 40 miles northeast of London, into a Christian family. In fact, both his father and grandfather were pastors. But his father met financial troubles and sent the young Charles to live with his grandparents from ages one to six. I don’t think this is an insignificant part of the story; don’t underestimate the effects of a good grandma and grandpa in the lives of our children. From their influence he emerged as “precocious,” learned to read, and first found Bunyan’s Pilgrim’s Progress (which he would read more than a hundred times). From his earliest days, he was unusually sharp, ahead of his age level, “always reading books” (Spurgeon: A Biography, 8). He returned home at age six and excelled at school in both math and reading. He was noticed for “his unusual mental ability and his rare clarity of speech” (10), including “his native audacity” (11), that is, his courage to say
content_zh:
我非常兴奋地向大家讲述上帝如何用一段简单的诗句, 从一段复杂的段落中, 他的故事是针对每个人的,但可能有一个特别的单词,可以和房间里的几个团体交谈. 一个是外行者,也就是在基督教部之外从事正常工作谋生的人。

没有神学院教育的人, 我们承认,这一系列的描述 4人谁是传道者。

现在,我们的系列有一个有趣的流传:首先,圣奥古斯丁, 然后,路德,他是一个奥古斯丁的修道士, 然后,约翰·邦扬,他最喜欢的书是路德对加拉提安的评论, 现在,查尔斯·斯普吉翁,他最喜欢的书是"邦扬朝圣者的进步"。

但我们系列的一个弱点(某种意义上的)就是他们都成了传教士。 我们并不期望你们都成为传教士;我们想做几个,但多数是外行,这很好。

现在,斯普吉翁被称为"道教的王子". 但是,在上帝的统治下,在斯普吉翁的故事里,英雄不是斯普吉翁,也不是一个受过训练,有报酬的传教士,而是一名外行人. 因此,斯普吉恩的故事有一个特别的词来形容那些愿意张开口子,说出自己对耶稣所了解的. Spurgeon的故事中也有一个针对青少年和年轻成年人的特殊词.

斯普吉安在15岁时开始信仰,在他这一天,这更像是年轻的成年. 然而,他的故事给那些已经不是孩子和还没有成年的人带来了挑战:青少年,大学生,研究生,甚至年轻专业人员.

不要让世界(或教会)降低你对于什么是可能的, 我的祷告是 上帝可能很乐意 给一些自己的引擎。 父母、大学员工和牧师经常帮助年轻的成年人并给予他们推动。

有时,上帝在青少年生活中很高兴给他们自己的引擎,他们不需要再再推了. 他们说:你们离我远点! 我要跟随耶稣。 你无法阻止我远离他, 这是上帝在15岁时为斯波克森所做的——他给了他自己的引擎. 我祈求他今天上午也乐意这么做

Spurgeon的故事又讲述了一个群体:那些在房间里愿意承认“我在这里,但我没有被拯救。 ” 两千年来,无所救护的人出于各种原因都出现在了教堂. 这是斯普吉恩的故事。 他在寻找。 周日早上,上帝破门而入时,他被解剖,在教堂里。

所以,如果你今天上午说,“我还没有解决我的罪恶和反抗上帝的问题,”或者“我还没有`拯救',或者“如果我今天在回家的路上死了,我也不会与我的造物主和睦相处,”这个故事有一个特别的词给你。 让我告诉你查理·斯波克森的事 他于1834年生于伦敦东北约40英里处,进入基督教家庭.

事实上,他的父亲和祖父都是牧师。 但是他的父亲遇到了财政上的困难,并派年轻的查尔斯从一到六岁就和外祖父母住在一起. 我并不认为这是故事的次要部分,

从他们的影响力中,他出现了“珍贵的,”学会了阅读,并首先发现了邦扬的"朝圣者进步"(他将读一百多遍)。 从他最初的年代起,他就异常尖锐地领先于他的年龄,"总是阅读书籍"("外科医生:一部传记",8). 他六岁回家,在学校数学和阅读方面都非常出色。

title_zh: 五个辅导失误和圣灵的帮助
content: As we were finishing a counseling session, Jill looked at me with concern, her eyebrows furrowed. “You got distracted,” she bluntly stated. Unfortunately, Jill was right. Just outside my workspace, several pastors gathered in the church office lobby, talking and laughing. I’d gotten sidetracked by the commotion. About 70 percent of me was attending to Jill, but 30 percent of my headspace had shifted to the lobby: What are they doing? What’s so funny? We live in a distractible culture. Between YouTube shorts and checking our email inboxes every hour, our minds wander quickly. Staying focused is a skill few truly master. But it’s essential if we’re going to care well for God’s people. Whether formally or informally, counseling another soul is a distinct privilege. Yet, too often, mistakes plague our conversations. Fortunately, getting distracted is one of several common mistakes that are correctable. After Jill’s jarring comment, I closed the window blinds (simple fix), talked to the staff about keeping the commotion down (another simple fix), recommitted to staying focused (possible, though it would be work), and prayed the Lord would renew my love for his sheep. What counseling mistakes are you prone to make? Take a quick check. Mistake 1: Fear of Man Charlotte shares about her struggles with her job. She dislikes her boss, and she’s weary of her work. Unfortunately, she often responds to her difficulties with sinful choices. This time, she lied to her boss to get out of an assignment. You sympathize with her frustrations but feel convinced you’ve got to speak up about her lying. Charlotte’s a Christian, and Scripture makes clear that because God never lies, Christ’s followers shouldn’t either (Colossians 3:9–10; Titus 1:2). Yet you hesitate. You know Charlotte will get angry, and your fears kick in. Why bother bringing it up? Lying is between her and God. Right now, she needs a friend. But you know if you don’t say something, Charlotte will eventually lie to her boss again. What should you do? Repent of your fear that causes you to avoid a difficult word. Confess your worry about speaking up to the Lord (Psalm 34:4). If you struggle with people-pleasing, then saying a difficult word will feel painful. Reframe your situation by putting the fear of God at the center of your thinking (Proverbs 29:25; Luke 12:4–5). If we fear God more than Charlotte, we won’t let Charlotte’s potential anger get in the way. My friend Jonathan Leeman calls the helper in this situation a “sin-absorber.” A true friend willingly absorbs the cost of another person’s sin for the sake of honoring Christ. Would you be willing to absorb Charlotte’s anger if it helps her address her lie? Mistake 2: Assumed Insight Angela and John have been married for 31 years. Sometimes John gets frustrated with Angela because she assumes what he’s thinking. “I know I’m not supposed to assume,” Angela would think, “but we’ve been together for a long time.” The more familiar you are with someone, the more you’re likely to get in trouble. Familiarity breeds assumptions . Think about your last conflict. How many assumptions did you make? Probably a few. Assumptions can create problems. Sometimes our assumptions are true, but often they’re not. If you’re prone to making assumptions, here’s how to stay away from trouble: Don’t overestimate your ability to size up a situation. Pride makes you think, “I know what’s going on.” Humility tells you, “Ask God for wisdom.” The humble recognize they’re not as smart as they think and must depend on the Lord for insight (James 1:5). After you’ve asked the Lord for help, test your assumptions. Don’t tolerate any of them. Check the validity of your assumptions by asking thoughtful, careful, and loving questions. Genuine curiosity will lead you to ask rather than assume.
